---
title: "The Half-Life of a Market Edge"
subtitle: "Post-publication alpha decay across 189 equity anomalies, 1926–2024"
author: "Mehmet Tuğsuz"
date: today
abstract: |
  Several hundred cross-sectional return predictors have been published since the 1980s.
  If they are compensation for risk, publication should not change them; if they are
  mispricing, publication is the moment enough capital learns about them to trade them
  away. Across the 189 usable signals in the Chen–Zimmermann universe (1926–2024,
  173,302 signal-months) the mean monthly long-short return falls 45% after publication
  and the median signal loses 53%, updating McLean and Pontiff (2016). The paper then
  tests, rather than asserts, the restriction that separates the arbitrage channel from
  the data-mining channel, and fails to reject equality — so the three-window design
  does not identify the channel on this universe. Two of the input series are rebuilt
  from raw CRSP as a check on the whole exercise.
---

def ym(mi):
    """Invert mi = year*12 + month.

    Month runs 1..12, so December has mi % 12 == 0 and mi // 12 == year + 1. Decoding
    with (mi // 12, mi % 12 or 12) is right eleven months out of twelve and files every

    """
    y, m = divmod(int(mi) - 1, 12)
    return y, m + 1

# The question {#sec-question}

A cross-sectional return predictor is a rule that sorts stocks on some characteristic
and goes long one end and short the other. Several hundred have been documented since
@banz1981, enough that @harvey2016 argue the conventional *t*-statistic hurdle of 2.0 is
far too low for a literature that has run this many tests, and @hou2020 find that a
majority do not survive careful replication.

That is a statement about the *past* of a signal. This project is about its *future*.
Take a predictor that was real in its original sample and ask what happens to it after
the paper appears. Two stories predict opposite things.

**Arbitrage.** The edge was mispricing. Publication makes it common knowledge, capital
arrives, the mispricing is traded away. @mclean2016 call this the out-of-sample
publication effect, and it is the mechanism in @shleifer1997: the edge shrinks, but not
necessarily to zero, because @grossman1980 requires a positive residual return to pay
for the arbitrage in the first place. A market in which every published edge went to
exactly zero would be one in which nobody was paid to look, and the edges would return.

**Data mining.** The edge was never there. The original sample was lucky — selected, over
fitted, or the survivor of a search across many candidate characteristics that were never
reported. Then the edge does not wait for publication to disappear; it is already gone
the moment you step outside the sample the author chose.

Both predict decay. They differ in *when*, and that is what makes the design in
@sec-design a test rather than a description.

# Data {#sec-data}

## The anomaly universe

@chen2022 reimplement several hundred published predictors from their original papers and
publish the resulting long-short portfolio return series together with a documentation
file recording, for each signal, the authors, the journal, the publication year, the
original sample window and the implementation parameters. Two files are used here, both
free:

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `PredictorLSretWide.csv` | monthly long-short returns, one column per signal |
| `SignalDoc.csv` | one row per signal: acronym, journal, `Year`, `SampleStartYear`, `SampleEndYear`, plus `Sign`, `Stock Weight`, `LS Quantile`, `Portfolio Period` |

**Release: October 2025, v2.0.0.** Most series run through December 2024;
option-implied-volatility predictors end December 2022. This is the first release
produced by the authors' Python translation rather than the original Stata code, and
`ChNAnalyst`, `PriceDelayTstat` and `Recomm_ShortInterest` carry revisions from bug fixes
in that translation. All three are in the universe below.

## Which signals enter, and why

Three filters, each of which changes the answer and therefore belongs in the text rather
than in a footnote.

1. **Predictors only.** The authors label some series as placebos — characteristics their
   own replication finds do not predict. Averaging those in would drag every window
   towards zero and flatter the decay.
2. **The paper's sample must end strictly before the paper appears.** If it does not,
   window 2 below has no months in it and the three-window design collapses to two.
3. **At least 24 monthly observations in *every* window.** Otherwise a signal can enter
   the post-publication average on the strength of three observations.

The third filter is what makes the headline comparison honest: the *same* signals appear
in all three windows, so the decline cannot be an artefact of the composition changing
between them.

::: {#panel .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"}
MIN_MONTHS = 24

d = doc[doc["Cat.Signal"] == "Predictor"].dropna(subset=["Year", "SampleEndYear"])
d = d[d["SampleEndYear"] < d["Year"]]                       # filter 2

usable = [c for c in rets.columns if c != "date" and c in set(d["Acronym"])]
long = (rets[["date"] + usable]
        .melt(id_vars="date", var_name="signal", value_name="ret")
        .dropna(subset=["ret"]))

meta = d.set_index("Acronym")[["Year", "SampleEndYear"]]
long["pub_year"] = long["signal"].map(meta["Year"]).astype(int)
long["samp_end"] = long["signal"].map(meta["SampleEndYear"]).astype(int)
long["year"] = long["date"].dt.year

long["window"] = np.select(
    [long["year"] <= long["samp_end"],
     (long["year"] > long["samp_end"]) & (long["year"] < long["pub_year"])],
    ["1_in_sample", "2_post_sample"],
    default="3_post_pub",
)
```
:::

# Design: three windows {#sec-design}

Cut each signal's history at two dates taken from its own paper:

| Window | Definition | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| 1. in-sample | year ≤ `SampleEndYear` | the edge as originally reported |
| 2. post-sample | `SampleEndYear` < year < `Year` | discovered, not yet public |
| 3. post-publication | year ≥ `Year` | public, and being traded on |

Window 2 is the whole design. Under the arbitrage story nothing happens until the paper
appears, so window 2 should look like window 1 and only window 3 falls. Under the
data-mining story window 2 is *already* lower, because stepping outside the author's
chosen sample is enough.

Write the estimand as a within-signal comparison of means. For signal $i$ let
$\mu_i^{(w)}$ be its mean long-short return in window $w$. Then

$$
\delta_1 \;=\; \mathbb{E}_i\!\left[\mu_i^{(2)} - \mu_i^{(1)}\right],
\qquad
\delta_2 \;=\; \mathbb{E}_i\!\left[\mu_i^{(3)} - \mu_i^{(1)}\right] ,
$$

and the quantity the two stories disagree about is the **increment**
$\delta_2 - \delta_1$: the part of the fall that arrives with publication rather than
with the end of the sample. Arbitrage predicts $\delta_1 \approx 0$ and
$\delta_2 - \delta_1 < 0$. Pure data mining predicts $\delta_1 < 0$ and
$\delta_2 - \delta_1 \approx 0$.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**What this design assumes.** $\delta_1$ and $\delta_2$ are causal effects of publication
only if the publication date is as good as randomly timed with respect to a signal's own
return path. That is not obviously true: authors submit when a result looks good, and
journals publish with a lag that is itself correlated with how strong the result is. The
design is therefore best read as an *event study with a pre-period*, not as a clean
experiment. @sec-next says what would tighten it.
:::

# The estimator {#sec-estimator}

## The regression

$$
r_{it} \;=\; \alpha_i \;+\; \beta_1 D^{\mathrm{post\text{-}sample}}_{it}
           \;+\; \beta_2 D^{\mathrm{post\text{-}pub}}_{it} \;+\; \varepsilon_{it}
$$ {#eq-main}

where $r_{it}$ is signal $i$'s long-short return in month $t$ in percent per month, the
two $D$ variables are the window indicators, and window 1 is the omitted category — so
$\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ are read against the in-sample mean. The signal fixed effect
$\alpha_i$ is what makes this a *within* comparison: without it, $\beta_2$ would partly
reflect the fact that signals published long ago are different signals from those
published recently.

## Absorbing the fixed effects

Rather than build 212 dummy columns, subtract each signal's own mean from
every variable:

$$
\tilde z_{it} \;=\; z_{it} - \bar z_i ,
\qquad \bar z_i = \frac{1}{T_i}\sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}_i} z_{it} .
$$

By the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem [@frisch1933; @lovell1963], regressing $\tilde r$ on
$\tilde D$ returns *numerically the same* $\hat\beta$ as the full dummy regression. This
is not an approximation and not a shortcut for speed alone: it is the statement that
$\beta$ is identified from variation over time within a signal.

## Clustering, and why by date

Two long-short portfolios in the same month are not independent draws. They are built
from the same stocks in the same market, so a month in which value and momentum both do
badly moves many of them at once. Clustering by **date** allows arbitrary correlation
within a month; clustering by signal would allow arbitrary correlation within a signal
across time, which is the wrong axis here [@petersen2009]. With
1\,188 months the cluster count is comfortably large, which matters
because cluster-robust inference is asymptotic in the number of clusters, not the number
of observations [@cameron2015].

Let $g = 1,\dots,G$ index months, $\tilde X_g$ the rows of the demeaned design matrix in
month $g$ and $\hat u_g$ the residuals there. The sandwich is

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta)
\;=\;
c \,\bigl(\tilde X'\tilde X\bigr)^{-1}
\Bigl[\textstyle\sum_{g=1}^{G} \bigl(\tilde X_g' \hat u_g\bigr)\bigl(\tilde X_g' \hat u_g\bigr)'\Bigr]
\bigl(\tilde X'\tilde X\bigr)^{-1},
\qquad
c \;=\; \frac{G}{G-1}\cdot\frac{n-1}{n-k} .
$$ {#eq-sandwich}

The bread is the usual $(X'X)^{-1}$; the meat is a sum of **outer products of
within-cluster score sums**, which is the whole content of clustering — scores are added
up inside a month before being squared, so correlation inside the month is absorbed
instead of assumed away. The finite-sample factor $c$ is the standard one. It does not
subtract the absorbed fixed effects from the degrees of freedom; at
173\,302 observations that changes the standard errors by about 0.1%.

::: {#estimator .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"}
def within(df, cols, by):
    """Demean `cols` within groups of `by`. FWL: identical to including group dummies."""
    return df[cols] - df.groupby(by)[cols].transform("mean")

def cluster_ols(y, X, cluster):
    """OLS with a cluster-robust covariance matrix, written out rather than imported."""
    XtX_inv = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)
    beta    = XtX_inv @ (X.T @ y)
    u       = X * (y - X @ beta)[:, None]

    codes = pd.factorize(cluster)[0]
    G     = codes.max() + 1
    meat  = np.zeros((X.shape[1], X.shape[1]))
    for g in range(G):                       # sum scores inside a cluster, then square
        s = u[codes == g].sum(axis=0)
        meat += np.outer(s, s)

    n, k = X.shape
    c    = (G / (G - 1)) * ((n - 1) / (n - k))
    V    = c * (XtX_inv @ meat @ XtX_inv)
    return beta, V, G

def fit(sub):
    s = sub.copy()
    s["post_sample"] = (s["window"] == "2_post_sample").astype(float)
    s["post_pub"]    = (s["window"] == "3_post_pub").astype(float)
    dm = within(s, ["ret", "post_sample", "post_pub"], "signal")
    y  = dm["ret"].to_numpy()
    X  = dm[["post_sample", "post_pub"]].to_numpy()
    return cluster_ols(y, X, s["date"].to_numpy())
```
:::

@mclean2016 report roughly −26% post-sample and −58% post-publication over 97 anomalies.
This universe is about twice as large and includes weaker and less-replicated signals,
which is the obvious first explanation for the smaller numbers and is testable by
re-running on their 97.

# What this does *not* show {#sec-restriction}

Read @tbl-panel quickly and the conclusion writes itself: $\beta_2$ is sharply estimated,
$\beta_1$ is not, therefore publication rather than overfitting is what kills the edge.
That conclusion does not survive a test.

"Publication matters over and above the end of the sample" is the restriction
$H_0: \beta_2 = \beta_1$, i.e. $R\beta = 0$ with $R = (-1,\;1)$. The standard error of
$R\hat\beta$ must come from the **same** clustered covariance matrix, and it is not the
sum of the two individual standard errors, because $\hat\beta_1$ and $\hat\beta_2$
covary:

$$
\mathrm{se}\!\left(\hat\beta_2 - \hat\beta_1\right)
= \sqrt{R \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta) R'}
= \sqrt{\widehat V_{11} + \widehat V_{22} - 2\widehat V_{12}} .
$$ {#eq-restriction}

Comparing two *t*-statistics — one significant, one not — is not a test of whether the
coefficients differ. @eq-restriction is.

::: {#restriction .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"}
R = np.array([-1.0, 1.0])

def restriction(beta, V):
    diff = R @ beta
    se   = np.sqrt(R @ V @ R)
    return diff, se, diff / se

diff_f, sed_f, td_f = restriction(beta_f, V_f)
diff_m, sed_m, td_m = restriction(beta_m, V_m)
corr_f = V_f[0, 1] / np.sqrt(V_f[0, 0] * V_f[1, 1])
```
:::


::: {#tbl-restriction .cell tbl-cap='Testing $\beta_2 = \beta_1$ on the same clustered covariance.' execution_count=12}

| Matched {N_MATCHED} | {diff_m:+.4f} | {sed_m:.4f} | {td_m:.2f} |
""")

The incremental effect of publication, over and above the decline that had already
happened by the time the original sample ended, is **not significant at the 5% level**
(|t| = 1\.67 against a 1.96 critical value). The estimated
correlation between $\hat\beta_1$ and $\hat\beta_2$ is
0\.33, which is why the difference is less precisely estimated than
$\hat\beta_2$ alone.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**The sentence not to write.** "Publication, not overfitting, is what kills the edge."
The point estimates are consistent with it. The data do not support it at conventional
levels, and the three-window design as run here does not separate the arbitrage channel
from the data-mining channel on this universe.

What can be said: the post-publication decline is precisely estimated, the post-sample
decline is not, and the difference between them is not sharp enough to claim. That is a
weaker headline and a stronger piece of work, because the restriction was tested rather
than eyeballed.
:::

# How much of this rests on someone else's numbers? {#sec-rebuild}

Everything above is computed from 189 return series that somebody else constructed. That
is a dependency, and an untested one. Two signals are therefore rebuilt from
security-level CRSP data and scored month by month against the published versions: `Size`,
about the simplest anomaly there is, and `Mom12m`, which has a formation window, a skip
month and overlapping holding periods and is therefore easy to get subtly wrong.

The pull (`03_crsp_pull.py`) and the rebuild (`04_build_anomalies.py`) need a WRDS
subscription. This section does not: it reads the committed result files.

## Portfolio construction, written out

At each formation month $m$ the cross-section is sorted on the signal and cut into
$n = 1/q$ buckets, where $q$ comes from `SignalDoc` — $q = 0.5$ for `Size` (halves, as in
@banz1981, who splits the market in two and does not sort deciles) and $q = 0.1$ for
`Mom12m`. For a bucket $B_m$ and a horizon $h$,

$$
\bar r^{\,B}_{m,h} \;=\;
\frac{\sum_{i \in B_m} w_{i,m}\, r_{i,\,m+h}}{\sum_{i \in B_m} w_{i,m}} ,
\qquad
\mathrm{LS}^{(h)}_{m} \;=\; s \cdot
\Bigl( \bar r^{\,\mathrm{top}}_{m,h} - \bar r^{\,\mathrm{bot}}_{m,h} \Bigr),
$$

with $w_{i,m} = 1$ for equal weighting and $w_{i,m} = \mathrm{mthcap}_{i,m}$ for value
weighting, and $s = \pm 1$ the sign from `SignalDoc` — **$s = -1$ for `Size`**, because
the anomaly is small minus big and reversing it produces a beautifully significant result
with the wrong label on it.

`Portfolio Period` is a holding period with overlapping cohorts [@jegadeesh1993]: the
return booked in calendar month $c$ averages the cohorts formed at
$c-1, \dots, c-H$,

$$
\mathrm{LS}_{c} \;=\; \frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H} \mathrm{LS}^{(h)}_{\,c-h} .
$$ {#eq-cohorts}

The momentum signal itself is the twelve-month return ending one month before formation:

$$
s^{\mathrm{mom}}_{i,m}
\;=\;
\exp\!\Biggl(\;\sum_{\tau = m-k-11}^{\,m-k} \log\bigl(1 + r_{i\tau}\bigr)\Biggr) - 1,
\qquad k = 1 ,
$$ {#eq-mom}

defined only where the stock has a contiguous monthly record across the window, and
`Size` is simply $s^{\mathrm{size}}_{i,m} = \log(\mathrm{mthcap}_{i,m})$.

## The verdict

::: {#rebuild-load .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="read the committed rebuild results"}
def load_rebuild(name, col):
    df = pd.read_csv(OUT / f"rebuild_{name}.csv")
    o  = df.dropna(subset=[col, "theirs"]).copy()
    o["gap"] = o[col] - o["theirs"]
    o["year"] = [ym(v)[0] for v in o["mi"]]
    return o

reb = {"Size": load_rebuild("Size", "mine"),
       "Mom12m": load_rebuild("Mom12m", "mine_hold1")}
COL = {"Size": "mine", "Mom12m": "mine_hold1"}

def gap_t(o):
    g = o["gap"].to_numpy()
    return g.mean(), g.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(g))

def corr(o, name):
    return float(np.corrcoef(o[COL[name]], o["theirs"])[0, 1])
```

## Is the momentum gap real?

::: {#gap-diagnostic .cell execution_count=16}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"}
o = reb["Mom12m"]
mg, sg = gap_t(o)
sd_gap = o["gap"].std(ddof=1)

# 1. thin pre-1963 data, when CRSP covers NYSE only?
pre, post = o[o["year"] < 1963], o[o["year"] >= 1963]
(mpre, spre), (mpost, spost) = gap_t(pre), gap_t(post)

# 2. a uniform implementation difference, present every month?
share_below = (o["gap"] < 0).mean()

# 3. or a tail?
worst   = o.reindex(o["gap"].abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index)
share60 = worst.head(60)["gap"].sum() / len(o) / mg
cut     = o["gap"].abs().quantile(0.90)
trim_all  = o[o["gap"].abs() <= cut]["gap"].mean()
cut_pre   = pre["gap"].abs().quantile(0.90)
trim_pre  = pre[pre["gap"].abs() <= cut_pre]["gap"].mean()
corr_abs  = float(np.corrcoef(o["gap"].abs(), o["theirs"].abs())[0, 1])
```
:::


**First, is it even distinguishable from zero?** A momentum long-short series is volatile
and so is the month-by-month difference between two implementations of one. The gap has a
standard deviation of 2\.03 %/month, so a mean of
\-0\.107 over 1\,174 months carries
**t = \-1\.82**. Before 1963 it is t = \-0\.74;
from 1963 on, t = \-1\.94. Neither era rejects equality.

**Hypothesis 1: thin early data.** CRSP covers NYSE only until mid-1962, so the natural
guess is that the gap sits before 1963 and the modern period replicates cleanly.
*Rejected.* The gap is \-0\.092 before 1963 and
\-0\.116 after — essentially identical.

**Hypothesis 2: a uniform implementation difference.** If a slightly different screen
produced a slightly different portfolio every month, the sign of the difference would be
persistent. *Rejected.* The rebuilt series is below the published one in
53\.0% of months, a coin flip.

**What it actually is: a tail.** The 60 largest-|gap| months — 5% of the sample — carry
100% of the mean difference. Trim the largest decile of months
and the full-sample gap falls to \-0\.051, while the pre-1963 gap
flips sign to \+0\.068. And the absolute gap correlates
0\.37 with the absolute size of that month's published return: the
discrepancy is largest exactly when momentum itself moves most.

These name themselves. 2009-03 is the worst month on record for momentum, and 1939-09 is
the outbreak-of-war rebound — both are momentum crashes in the sense of @daniel2016, when
past losers surge and the extreme deciles turn over violently. In exactly those months a
single imputed price, or one stock that delists in the middle of a holding period, moves a
bucket mean by percentage points, and two implementations of a decile sort must part
company. @shumway1997 is the classic statement of how much the treatment of disappearing
stocks matters.

**The line not crossed.** No screen variants were tried. Closing the remaining
0\.107 %/month by searching filter combinations until the number
matches would be curve-fitting the replication itself — the same behaviour this project
exists to measure. The position without it is defensible: one signal reproduces exactly,
the other reproduces to within sampling error.
:::

## The bug this caught, and why correlation hid it {#sec-skip}

`SignalDoc` defines `Mom12m` over "months t-12 and t-1". **Month $t$ is excluded** — the
$k = 1$ in @eq-mom. The first implementation used $m-11,\dots,m$ instead, which pulls
short-term reversal [@jegadeesh1990] into a momentum signal: last month's return is
negatively autocorrelated, so including it does not add noise, it adds an effect of the
opposite sign.

::: {#skip .cell execution_count=18}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"}
# `mine` and `mine_noskip` are both the documented three-month holding period. They
# differ in one thing only: whether month t is inside the formation window. Compare them
# on the same rows, so the holding period cannot be doing the work.
ns = (pd.read_csv(OUT / "rebuild_Mom12m.csv")
        .dropna(subset=["mine", "mine_noskip", "theirs"]))
mean_skip   = ns["mine"].mean()
mean_noskip = ns["mine_noskip"].mean()
mean_theirs = ns["theirs"].mean()
corr_noskip = float(np.corrcoef(ns["mine_noskip"], ns["theirs"])[0, 1])
```
:::


Holding everything else fixed at the documented three-month holding period, dropping the
skip takes the long-short mean from 0\.652 to
0\.459 %/month, against a published
0\.899. Rebalanced monthly, where no cohort skips at all, it went
to −0.009 %/month: the premium gone entirely.

**And the correlation never flinched: 0\.974, peaking at lag 0.**
That is the lesson worth keeping. A correlation confirms that the wiring is right and the
timing is right; it rules out a merge error or an off-by-one in the calendar. It says
nothing about whether the *signal definition* is right, because a wrong window is still
mostly the same portfolio. Only the level catches this.

# What the design cannot do, and what comes next {#sec-next}

## Two-way fixed effects under staggered treatment

Publication arrives at a different date for every signal, so @eq-main is a two-way fixed
effects regression with staggered adoption. @goodmanbacon2021 shows that such an estimator
is a variance-weighted average of all possible two-group comparisons, **including
comparisons that use already-treated signals as controls for later-treated ones**. When the
treatment effect varies across signals or evolves over time — and decay that continues for
years after publication is precisely a treatment effect that evolves — those comparisons
enter with the wrong sign and the weighted average need not lie inside the range of the
true effects [@dechaisemartin2020].

That is a concrete reason to doubt $\hat\beta_2$ as a causal estimate, separate from the
identification worry in @sec-design. The repairs are known: @callaway2021 estimate group-
time effects using only not-yet-treated units as controls, @sun2021 do the interaction-
weighted version for event studies, and @borusyak2024 give the efficient imputation
estimator. @roth2023 survey the choice. **This is the next thing to build**, and it should
change the number.

## Why not regression discontinuity

Publication is a date, which invites the thought that a discontinuity design applies. It
does not. RDD needs a running variable with a cutoff and units that cannot precisely
manipulate their position around it. Here the "running variable" is calendar time, the
cutoff is anticipated — working papers circulate for years before a journal issue appears —
and authors have some control over timing. Anticipation alone is fatal: informed traders
acting on a working paper push part of the decay *before* the event, which biases the
estimate towards zero and makes the post-publication decline a **lower bound** on the true
one. The honest labels are interrupted time series and event study; the sharper version is
staggered difference-in-differences, above.

## How fast, and to what floor

A three-window average says the edge fell. It does not say how quickly, or whether it fell
to zero. Two routes:

$$
\alpha_t \;=\; \phi + (\alpha_0 - \phi)\,e^{-\lambda t}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\text{half-life} \;=\; \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda},
$$

fitted per signal by nonlinear least squares, is the simple version, and $\phi$ is the
**floor** — which @grossman1980 says should be strictly positive, so estimating it is a
test of that prediction rather than an accounting exercise. The upgrade is a local-level
state-space model,

$$
r_t = \alpha_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad
\alpha_t = \alpha_{t-1} + \eta_t, \qquad
\varepsilon_t \sim N(0,\sigma^2_\varepsilon),\;\; \eta_t \sim N(0,\sigma^2_\eta),
$$

estimated by the Kalman filter and smoother [@durbin2012], which returns an $\alpha_t$ path
with a credible interval instead of a curve fitted by eye. A Markov-switching version
[@hamilton1989] would give a "probability the edge is still alive" series.

## Who dies fast, and why

The cross-sectional question is where the arbitrage story becomes falsifiable: decay should
be fastest where arbitrage is cheapest. The proxies — Amihud illiquidity [@amihud2002],
market capitalisation, idiosyncratic volatility, short interest, institutional ownership —
are all computable from the CRSP panel this project already built, which is the reason
@sec-rebuild exists. Independently, `contrib.global_factor` [@jensen2023] carries 153
characteristics across 93 countries, which turns the same hypothesis into a cross-country
test with completely different identifying variation.
